Q: Informix multiple joins A:

You need to use the standard join syntax for this. Your query should look like:

SELECT DISTINCT x.xfertype, x.app_type, x.service_type, x.lang,x.area_type,
       x.area_value, x.module, x.field1, x.field2, x.disabled,
       a.frames, a.allocs, a.term_id,
       t.term,c.center_id, c.center_name,a.message_id, x.field3, x.apn_type,x.global,
       a.icm, s.group_name
FROM test_xfertypes x join
     test_allocation a
     on a.xfertype = x.xfertype join
     test_terms t
     on a.term_id = t.term_id join
     test_callcenter c
     on t.center_id = c.center_id

You can left join another table just by adding:

left outer join test_routing_groups s
on x.area_value IN (s.area_id)

You can also use an x.area_value = s.area_id rather than the IN clause.

Q: Passwords get lost after deployment A:

Here is a few reasons:

  1. If the password or user name text box name changes, then the browser will disassociate the login with the web site.

Original syntax in razor:

@Html.PasswordFor(model => model.**Password**)

New password box:

@Html.PasswordFor(model => model.**MyPassword**)

  1. If the view changes name or the login occurs in a new view then the browser will disassociate the password with the web site

  2. You also need to check the expiration of the browser cache.

  3. Check for security updates on the browser

Q: SQL Server stalls for ten minutes A:

ASP.NET hangs can happen for a variety of reasons. Typically you get Connection or Command timeouts when you have problems with SQL not hangs.

You're much better off

  • Grabbing the Debugging Tools for Windows
  • Use AdPlus to grab a memory dump (adplus -hang -pn processname.exe) or DebugDiag and setup a dump rule
  • Use WinDbg (or VS 2010 for 4.0 framework) (after you set up a symbol cache) and start examining what's happening using !threads or !dumpheap -stat to inspect the threads and the heap objects.

Please note debugging production issues is very hard and WinDbg is not a friendly tool but guessing and looking at logs is even less so.

Q: What are common architectural patterns used in modern web applications A:

It's tempting to choose The One True Architecture that applies to every project. The fact is we continually make tradeoffs between complexity, scalability, testability, flexibility, adaptability, performance, robustness, and ease of maintenance. I have found some common threads, though:

  • A testable application can be evolved, and automated testing with a good CI/CD pipeline is how you achieve this.
  • Structure your application to be testable, and isolate the infrastructure code from the business logic.
  • The user interface changes more than anything, so this is another layer worth isolating.
  • Separation of Concerns will save you many migraines; this isn't so much a pattern as it is a guiding principle.
  • You'll encounter MVC in Web APIs, though it's debatable if it's really model-view-controller in the classical sense.
  • Frontend frameworks tend to favor MVVM or MVP, and reactive programming.
  • Dependency injection is used everywhere and facilitates testability.
  • Beware of vendor lock-in. It can be worthwhile to create an application-specific layer of abstraction over top of the code you don't control.
  • Separate user interface logic, business logic, and data access logic. This separation frequently feels like overhead right up until it doesn't, and then you're glad those things are separated.
  • Domain-driven design is not architecture; it's an approach to designing a software system that puts business terminology at the forefront, and forces you to think about how organizations and business processes are subdivided. DDD does not prescribe a pattern for organizing files and software layers, no matter what people might say. It involves how you think about the software design process, not about architecture.
  • Designing your web APIs to be a chain reaction of HTTP calls just makes your whole ecosystem a house of cards. One failed call brings the whole house down.
  • Strategically introduce message queues and eventual consistency to break up those chains of calls.
  • And then learn that this probably models real business processes better than ACID-compliant transactions, but adds complexity (see first paragraph).

You'll see Onion Architecture and Clean Architecture mentioned numerous times. The biggest benefit to onion architecture is orienting the application around core business rules and forcing infrastructure code to the outside of the dependency tree. The biggest benefit of clean architecture is that someone took onion architecture, added a lot more buzzwords, and then wrote a book about it. They're earning an honest living, so I can't judge.

I know my answer is a hot mess, but this is our reality.
